You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:

 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [

     ],

    },
    {

      "out",

     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {

     "nodes": [
      "pzp",

     ],

    },
    {

    },
    {

     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: $V_{out,min} \ge 1.8V$, $V_{out,max} \le 3.6V$, Ripple $\le 0.02V$, Startup $t_{up} \le 0.15s$, Settled $dv \le 0.01V$.
    *   Best design so far: `SSHI_Bridge_Clamp` (Score 33.96).
    *   `SSHI_Bridge_Clamp` failures:
        *   Startup: $S_2 (0.17s)$, $S_4 (0.25s)$, $S_5 (0.19s)$, $S_6 (0.16s)$. All are slightly above $0.15s$.
        *   Ripple: $S_3 (27mV)$ is slightly above $20mV$.
    *   Observation: The voltage $V_{avg}$ is very high ($\approx 3.4V$), which is close to the $3.6V$ limit. This high voltage is caused by the SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) mechanism and the Zener clamp.
    *   The startup issue suggests the storage capacitor $C_1$ might be too large, slowing down the initial rise, OR the power delivered at low voltage is insufficient.
    *   The ripple issue on $S_3$ (light load) suggests $C_1$ might be too small for the pulses, but the startup issue suggests $C_1$ is too large. Wait, $S_3$ is a *light load* ($RL = 2200 k\Omega$), so the discharge is slow. The ripple is likely due to the charging pulses themselves.

    *   `SSHI_Bridge_Clamp` is essentially an SSHI circuit with a full-bridge rectifier and a Zener clamp.
    *   The SSHI part (L1, S1, G1) flips the piezo voltage, increasing the energy extracted per cycle.
    *   The full-bridge (D1-D4) rectifies this flipped voltage.
    *   The Zener (D5) prevents overvoltage.

    *   *Problem 1: Startup ($t_{up} > 0.15s$)*.
        *   Current $C_1 = 2.2\mu F$.
        *   To reach $1.8V$ faster, we either need more current or less capacitance.
        *   However, the power extracted by SSHI is high (as seen in the screen results: $>200\%$ of load need).
        *   The bottleneck for startup might be the diode drops in the bridge rectifier.
    *   *Problem 2: Ripple ($\approx 27mV$ on S3)*.
        *   Ripple in these systems usually comes from the discrete nature of the SSHI charge packets.
        *   $V_{pp} = \Delta Q / C_1$. To reduce $V_{pp}$, we need larger $C_1$.
    *   *Conflict:* Startup wants smaller $C_1$, Ripple wants larger $C_1$.
    *   *Observation:* $V_{avg}$ is $\approx 3.4V$. We have a lot of "headroom" between $1.8V$ and $3.4V$. If we can shift the operating point slightly lower, or increase the efficiency at low voltage, we might solve startup.
    *   *Alternative for Startup:* The full-bridge rectifier has two diode drops in the charging path. If we use a half-bridge or a different rectification scheme, can we improve it? But the `SSHI_Bridge_Clamp` is already performing well.

    *   What if we use a *Synchronous Rectifier*? Instead of diodes, use switches. But we only have 4 switches total and 2 SYNCs.
    *   Wait, the `SSHI_Bridge_Clamp` uses a full-bridge (4 diodes) and one SSHI switch (1 switch). Total 5 components + L, C, Zener.
    *   Can we improve the startup by reducing the diode drops?
    *   Maybe a *Charge Pump* or a *Voltage Multiplier*? No, that would likely increase $V_{max}$ too much.
    *   What if we use a *parallel* capacitor or a different topology?
    *   Let's consider the "Cold Start" problem. At $t=0$, $V_{out}=0$. The diodes $D_1-D_4$ are the only path.

    *   If $C_1$ is too large for startup but too small for ripple, maybe we need a way to charge $C_1$ faster initially.
    *   Actually, look at $S_4$ startup ($0.247s$). $S_4$ is "weak excitation".
    *   Looking at $S_3$ ripple ($27mV$). $S_3$ is "strong excitation, light load".
    *   If we increase $C_1$ to fix $S_3$ ripple, $S_4$ startup will get even worse.
    *   If we decrease $C_1$ to fix $S_4$ startup, $S_3$ ripple will get worse.
    *   This suggests we need a more efficient energy transfer during the initial phase or a way to decouple the ripple-filtering capacitance from the startup-limiting capacitance.

    *   Could we use a different inductor-based topology?
    *   A "Buck-Boost" style SSHI?
    *   The current SSHI flips $V_{pzp}$ across $C_p$. The energy is then rectified.
    *   The `SSHI_Bridge_Clamp` is effectively: $\text{Piezo} \to \text{SSHI} \to \text{Full Bridge} \to C_{out}$.
    *   What if we put the inductor *after* the rectifier? (Not standard SSHI).
    *   What if we use a *Half-Bridge* SSHI but with a better rectification?
    *   Wait, look at the `HalfBridge_SSHI_Clamp` (Design 1). It failed ripple and startup significantly. The full bridge is definitely better for energy extraction.

    *   The startup time $t_{up}$ is the time to reach $1.8V$.
    *   The power $P_{load}$ is measured at the settled state.
    *   The screen result for `SSHI_Bridge_Clamp` shows it delivers $31.4 \mu W$ on $S_4$ (where only $3.24 \mu W$ is needed).
    *   If it delivers $10\times$ the required power, why is startup so slow?
    *   $V_{out}$ rises linearly: $dV/dt = I_{avg} / C_1$.
    *   $I_{avg} \approx P / V_{out}$.
    *   $t_{up} \approx \int (C_1 / I_{avg}) dV$.
    *   If $C_1 = 2.2\mu F$, $V = 1.8V$, $P = 31.4 \mu W$, then $I_{avg} \approx 17 \mu A$.
    *   $t \approx (2.2\mu F \cdot 1.8V) / 17\mu A \approx 0.23s$.
    *   This matches the $S_4$ startup result ($0.247s$).
    *   To get $t_{up} < 0.15s$, we must reduce $C_1$ to about $1.3\mu F$.
    *   But if we reduce $C_1$ to $1.3\mu F$, the ripple $V_{pp} = \Delta Q / C_1$ will increase.
    *   $\Delta Q$ for $S_3$ (strong excitation) is higher. $V_{pp}$ is already $27mV$ with $2.2\mu F$. With $1.3\mu F$, $V_{pp}$ will be $\approx 27 \cdot (2.2/1.3) \approx 45mV$. This fails the ripple check ($20mV$).

    *   *Conclusion:* We need to deliver *more* power during startup or reduce the ripple without increasing $C_1$.
    *   How to reduce ripple without increasing $C_1$?
        *   Increase the frequency of charging pulses? (Not possible, $f$ is fixed).
        *   Reduce the charge per pulse $\Delta Q$? (This means less energy extraction).
        *   Use an LC filter? (An inductor between the rectifier and $C_{out}$).

    *   *Adding an LC filter:*
        *   $\text{Rectifier} \to L_{filter} \to C_{out}$.
        *   This would smooth the current pulses, reducing $V_{pp}$ on $C_{out}$ without needing a massive $C_1$.
        *   This allows $C_1$ to be small enough for fast startup.

    *   Topology: `SSHI_Bridge_LC_Filter`
    *   L1, S1, G1: SSHI (same as before).
    *   D1-D4: Full Bridge.
    *   L2: Filter inductor between the bridge output and $C_{out}$.
    *   C1: Storage capacitor.
    *   D5: Zener clamp (should be after L2, at the `out` node).

    *   *Wait, let's refine the connection:*
        *   Piezo nodes: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        *   SSHI: `pzp` -> `L1` -> `n1`, `n1` -> `S1` -> `pzn`.
        *   Bridge:
            *   `D1`: `pzp` -> `n_rect_pos`
            *   `D2`: `pzn` -> `n_rect_pos`
            *   `D3`: `0` -> `pzp`
            *   `D4`: `0` -> `pzn`
            *   Wait, that's not a full bridge. A standard full bridge for a piezo:
                *   D1: `pzp` -> `out`
                *   D2: `pzn` -> `out`
                *   D3: `0` -> `pzp`
                *   D4: `0` -> `pzn`
                *   (This is what `SSHI_Bridge_Clamp` used).
        *   To add an LC filter, we need a node between the bridge and $C_{out}$:
            *   `D1`: `pzp` -> `n_filter`
            *   `D2`: `pzn` -> `n_filter`
            *   `D3`: `0` -> `pzp`
            *   `D4`: `0` -> `pzn`
            *   `L2`: `n_filter` -> `out`
            *   `C1`: `out` -> `0`
            *   `D5`: `0` -> `out` (Zener)
    *   *Wait*, the bridge diodes $D_3, D_4$ are connected to `pzp` and `pzn`. The return path is from `0` to the piezo. This is a standard bridge.
    *   Let's check the components count:
        *   L1 (SSHI), S1 (SSHI), G1 (SYNC): 3
        *   D1, D2, D3, D4 (Bridge): 4
        *   L2 (Filter): 1
        *   C1 (Storage): 1
        *   D5 (Zener): 1
        *   Total: 10 components. (Limit is 16).

    *   L2 should be small enough not to block DC but large enough to filter the $200\text{Hz}$ (2x frequency) pulses.
    *   $f_{ripple} = 200\text{Hz}$. $L = 10\text{mH}, C = 2.2\mu F \to f_c = 1 / (2\pi\sqrt{LC}) \approx 1070\text{Hz}$.
    *   This should provide significant attenuation.

    *   The `SSHI_Bridge_Clamp` had $V_{avg} \approx 3.4V$.
    *   The Zener `DZ33` clamps at $3.3V$.
    *   The load $R_L$ is from `out` to `0`.
    *   With $L_2$ in series, the voltage $V_{out}$ will be determined by the balance of extracted power and load power.
    *   One concern: $L_2$ adds series resistance ($2\Omega + 5\Omega/\text{mH}$). For $10\text{mH}$, $R_{series} = 52\Omega$. This is negligible compared to $R_L (150\text{k}\Omega)$.

    *   S3: Strong excitation, light load ($RL = 2200\text{k}$).
    *   $C_1$ can be smaller (e.g., $1\mu F$) to speed up startup for S2, S4, S5, S6.
    *   The $L_2 C_1$ filter will handle the ripple.
    *   Startup $t_{up}$ for $S_4$ (worst case):
        *   $P \approx 31\mu W$, $V_{out} = 1.8V$, $C_1 = 1\mu F$.
        *   $t_{up} \approx (1\mu F \cdot 1.8V) / 17\mu A \approx 0.105s$.
        *   This is well within the $0.15s$ limit.

    *   The current bridge in `SSHI_Bridge_Clamp` was:
        `D1: pzp -> out`
        `D2: pzn -> out`
        `D3: 0 -> pzp`
        `D4: 0 -> pzn`
    *   This is a symmetric bridge.
    *   Let's use it with the filter:
        `D1: pzp -> n_filter`
